newsitem.title: USA: Famed NY library room to shut for two years.
newsitem.headline: Famed NY library room to shut for two years.

text.p: Author E.L. Doctorow wrote in the New York Public Library's famous reading room, inventor Edwin Land dreamed up a new kind of camera and actress Lillian Gish researched roles there.
Now New Yorkers famous and not-so-famous will have to do without the elegant, cavernous reading room. It is closing on Monday for a two-year renovation.
Library officials hasten to say the reading room's facilities will be transferred to another, smaller room in the interim.
But for some, the change will be devastating.

"It's a big loss for me. I've been coming here 20 years," said playwright Mac Wellman, as he wrote a chapter of his novel longhand into a notebook. He was one of hundreds of people who sat at the room's long tables on a hot summer day.
"The room is full of ghosts, full of history," he said. "It has a special feeling. It's not too quiet. It's not too removed from the world."
The renovation is designed both to modernise the room and restore it to its original beaux-arts elegance.

The library first opened its doors onto Fifth Avenue, guarded by the carved lions Patience and Fortitude, in 1911. Not far away is mammoth Grand Central Terminal, which is undergoing its own renovation.
The landmark library's reading room is as long as an American football field and one of the largest uncolumned interior spaces in New York City.
Its 52-foot (16-metre) ceilings are covered with ornate carvings and painted murals, and its arched windows reach 17 feet (5 metres) high.

The renovation will clean the last of the World War Two black-out paint from those windows, wire its oak tables to accomodate laptop computers, improve the lighting, speed up the book retrieval system and move the clutter of computer terminals, printers and copiers to tidier spaces.
"The room has gotten tacky," admitted library spokeswoman Nancy Donner, who promised, "It's going to look old but work like new."
The renovation comes courtesy of an anonymous $15 million donation from "a wonderful, extraordinary person," said Paul LeClerc, president of the New York Public Library.
Not quite everyone agrees with that assessment of the anonymous donor.
"I know why he's staying anonymous. He doesn't want people coming and complaining," groused Maria Naylor as she pored over a book of mediaeval art. "What's wrong with this room? It's fine."

Official library lore holds that great thoughts have been thought in the reading room by such thinkers as Land, who designed the polariser for the Polaroid Land camera, and Chester Carlson, the inventor of the Xerox copier, who researched photoconductivity.
The roster of writers includes not just Doctorow but John Updike, Norman Mailer, Isaac Bashevis Singer and Alfred Kazin.
Then there are those whose work never received any acclaim.

"There used to be an elderly man who sat and wrote endless loops on pieces of paper. He was here about 10 years," said Wellman, the playwright and novelist. "I figure that's just as good as what I do."
